newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon now favorite to win Hughes bid.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon now favorite to win Hughes bid.

text.p: Defence industry powerhouse Raytheon Corp. appeared to be emerging Monday as the winner in the bidding war for Hughes Electronics Corp.'s highly coveted missile and radar business, according to people familiar with the situation.

The Lexington, Mass.-based defence electronics maker has been battling with Los Angeles rival Northrop Grumman Corp. for the unit, widely regarded as one of the last big trophies in the rapidly consolidating defence industry.
The winner of the bidding war will emerge as the premier firm in the defence electronics business.
Both Raytheon and Northrop Grumman are believed to have submitted bids between $9.5 billion and $10.4 billion to Hughes parent General Motors Corp. for consideration.
But, according to an investment banker familar with the negotiations, Northrop officials have started to believe GM was leaning toward Raytheon.

"People at Northrop who I spoke to this morning confirmed ... that they feel like they are running behind," the banker said. "They basically feel they've had a lack of meetings (with General Motors). You can tell in these things whether you're being pumped to be the leader or not."
All the companies involved declined to comment Monday.
GM wants to avoid having to pay the hefty capital gains taxes that would result from a cash sale of Hughes by having El Segundo, Calif.-based Hughes issue up to $5 billion in debt.
The acquiring company would assume that debt with the purchase, and would make up the rest of the sale price with shares of its own stock.
Analysts said the tricky financial structure meant the company with the brightest future would offer GM the best deal.

"Northrop needs it (the purchase) the most," the investment banker said, "The problem is it's easier for Raytheon to do it because they have the better balance sheet and (Raytheon shares) would trade better."
Paul Nisbet, a defence analyst with JSA Research, agreed.
"Price is only a secondary concern," he said, adding that loading up the winning bidder with too much debt would only impair the future value of that company's stock price.
"It sure seems it's Raytheon. That's the only one that really makes sense in a stock swap situation," Nisbet said. Analysts said Raytheon was the likely winner.
"Everybody seems to think that Raytheon, if they don't blow their credit rating, has the inside track on this thing," said Thomas Meagher of brokerage Ferris, Baker, Watts.
Last week, Raytheon agreed to buy Texas Instruments Inc.'s defence assets for $2.95 billion in a move that analysts said further strenghtened any advantages it would gain from buying the Hughes unit.
A GM spokeswoman declined to comment on the bidding war or on whether GM planned any special board meetings this week.
GM Chairman Jack Smith said Sunday the board had no plans to meet Monday or Tuesday. He added that GM was "just trying to get top dollar" for the Hughes assets.
A source close to the situation said GM's board could meet via a telephone conference to consider and approve a deal. An announcement was not expected before the end of the week.
"They have got some credit agency concerns about this transaction that is slowing this down," said Roger Threlfall, an analyst at investment bank J.P. Morgan. "It's a very complex transaction."

Hughes Chairman Michael Armstrong is scheduled to make a speech Wednesday at the Economic Club of Detroit, but a Hughes source said Armstrong would not announce or discuss a deal and said the speech did not mean a deal is imminent.

At stake are Hughes businesses with annual revenues of about $6.2 billion. The assets include missile systems, radar and communications electronics, air traffic control systems and an electro-optical devices unit.
By selling the business, GM's Hughes will be able to focus on more promising areas, such as satellites and satellite television.
The deal would be one of the biggest ever in the industry, falling short only of the $14.6 billion takeover of McDonnell Douglas Corp. by Boeing Co.

GM's H class stock, which reflects the performance of Hughes Electronics, was unchanged at $63.125 on the New York Stock Exchange. Raytheon was unchanged at $47.25, and Northrop rose 50 cents to $78.25, both on the NYSE.
